content: Cullin-5 (CUL5) is a protein encoded by the CUL5 gene in humans. Discovery The mammalian product of the CUL5 gene was initially identified through expression cloning. This discovery was based on the protein's ability to mobilize intracellular calcium in response to the peptide hormone arginine vasopressin. At the time of its discovery, it was named VACM-1, which stands for vasopressin-activated, calcium-mobilizing receptor. Subsequent research revealed that VACM-1 is homologous to the Cullin family of proteins, leading to its renaming as CUL5. Tissue Distribution Studies have demonstrated that the CUL5 protein is most abundantly expressed in cardiac and skeletal tissues. It is also specifically expressed in vascular endothelial cells and renal collecting tubules. Function CUL5 plays a role in inhibiting cellular proliferation. This function is thought to be mediated through its involvement in the SOCS/BC-box/eloBC/CUL5/RING E3 ligase complex, which is a component of the ubiquitin-proteasome system responsible for protein degradation. Additionally, one study has shown that CUL5 is involved in the Reelin signaling cascade. In this context, it participates in the degradation of DAB1, thereby maintaining the negative feedback mechanism of Reelin signaling during corticogenesis. Interactions CUL5 has been shown to interact with RBX1, a key component of the E3 ubiquitin ligase complex.
